title: "Then Stop Being Emperor"
text:
The Roman emperor Hadrian, who ruled from 117 to 138, spent much of his reign traveling around the empire, inspecting provinces and armies and meeting the people he governed.

The historian Cassius Dio, writing about a century later, tells a short story about one of these journeys. As Hadrian was passing along a road, a woman came up and asked him to hear a request. He was busy and told her that he had no time. She called after him: "Then stop being emperor." Hadrian turned around, Dio says, and gave her a hearing.

Dio tells the story as an example of the emperor's attention to ordinary subjects. He also mentions that Hadrian took care over the administration of justice, sat with advisers when he judged cases, and dealt with many matters personally. The woman's sharp answer survived because the emperor took it as a fair rebuke rather than an insult.
lesson: If you hold a position of responsibility, listening to the people it affects is the job, not an interruption of it.
source: Cassius Dio, Roman History, Book 69, chapter 6
caveat: A very similar story is told of earlier kings, such as Philip II of Macedon, so it may be a traveling anecdote.
